title: Country Life
description: Ten stories, columns and reports about life in the American countryside: dairy farms, apple harvests, county fairs, ranches and city families who move to the country.

lessons.title: The Cows That Send Messages
lessons.summary: A Wisconsin farmer converts her old barn into a modern milking center and learns to read her cows on a smartphone.
lessons.text:
Karen Olson has milked cows on her family's farm in Wisconsin for thirty years. For most of those years, the work was hard and the days were long. Every morning at five, in the cold gray light, she walked across the yard to the barn, and every evening she did the same thing again.

Two years ago, Karen and her son, Erik, converted the old barn into a modern milking center. Where there had once been dark wooden walls and narrow stalls, there were now clean white floors, bright lights and a milking robot. The converted barn cost most of the family's savings, but Karen does not regret it.

Each cow now wears a small sensor around her neck. The sensor counts her steps, measures how much she eats and notices when she is not feeling well. Another sensor inside the robot measures her milk. Together, the sensors send a continuous stream of information to a computer in the farm office. The stream is continuous, day and night, so Karen always knows how her cows are doing.

At first, Karen found the system difficult. The interface on the office computer was full of tiny numbers and gray boxes. Erik, who is twenty-four, showed her how to use a simpler interface on her smartphone. Now she carries her smartphone everywhere, even into the fields. To unlock the app, she types a password. Erik chose the password for her, and she has written it on a card that she keeps in the kitchen drawer. "A password only helps if you can remember it," she says with a smile.

Once the app is unlocked, Karen can see each cow's name, her milk and her steps for the day. The app also shows statistical charts: the average amount of milk per cow, the average for the whole farm, and how these numbers change from month to month. Karen was never fond of math at school, but she has come to enjoy this statistical picture of her farm. Last spring, the charts showed her that one group of cows gave more milk after she changed their food.

The cows seem to like the new system, too. They walk to the robot whenever they want to be milked, often three times a day instead of two. Calm cows are productive cows, and the farm is now more productive than ever. However, Karen believes the most productive change has happened in her own life. She no longer gets up at five. Instead, she checks her smartphone over a cup of coffee and walks out to the cows when the sun is up.

Questions:
What did Karen and Erik do two years ago?
They converted the old barn into a modern milking center.
What does the sensor on each cow do?
It counts her steps, measures how much she eats and notices when she is not feeling well.
How does Karen unlock the app on her smartphone?
She types a password, which Erik chose for her.
What did the statistical charts show Karen last spring?
They showed her that one group of cows gave more milk after she changed their food.
Why is the farm more productive now?
The cows are calm, and they are milked more often, sometimes three times a day.

lessons.title: A Day Among the Apple Trees
lessons.summary: Lily helps her grandfather with the apple harvest, learns his recipe for cider and has a small accident in the cellar.
lessons.text:
Last October, Lily spent a weekend helping her grandfather, Walter, with the apple harvest. Walter's trees grew on a gentle hill, and at the bottom of the hill a narrow brook ran over smooth stones. On the first morning, the air was cool and pleasant, and the only sounds were the birds and the brook.

Before they started, Walter gave Lily a pair of thick gloves. "Wear your gloves all day," he said. "The branches are rough, and there are insects everywhere at this time of year." Lily put on the gloves, which were much too big for her, and climbed the ladder. Small insects flew around the fallen fruit on the grass, but they did not bother her. Walter explained that most of the insects among his trees were harmless, and some of them even helped the trees.

They picked two kinds of apples. The first kind was red and sweet. Lily bit into one, and its white flesh was firm and full of juice. The second kind was small and green, with hard flesh and a very bitter taste. Lily tasted one and made a face. "Nobody eats those," Walter laughed. "They are too bitter on their own. But a mixture of sweet and bitter apples makes the best cider." He told her that his mixture was an old family recipe: three baskets of sweet apples to one basket of bitter ones.

In the afternoon, they carried the baskets down to the cellar under the house. The walls of the cellar were lined with wooden shelves, and each shelf had a label: "sweet," "bitter" or "for pies." Lily was putting a full basket on the top shelf when she accidentally knocked over a bucket of fresh apple juice. The juice spilled across the floor and ran under the shelves. Lily felt terrible, but Walter only smiled. "Everyone spills something during the harvest," he said. "Last year I spilled a whole bucket myself." Together they cleaned the floor, and then Walter accidentally stepped in the last wet spot, which made them both laugh.

That evening, they sat outside and drank warm cider made from last year's mixture. The air smelled of apples, the brook was still running quietly at the bottom of the hill, and Lily thought it had been the most pleasant day of her whole year.

Questions:
Why did Walter give Lily gloves?
He gave her gloves because the branches were rough and there were insects everywhere.
What was the flesh of the red apples like?
Its white flesh was firm, sweet and full of juice.
Why does nobody eat the green apples on their own?
Nobody eats them because they are too bitter.
What is Walter's mixture for cider?
It is three baskets of sweet apples to one basket of bitter ones.
What happened in the cellar?
Lily accidentally knocked over a bucket, and the juice spilled across the floor.

lessons.title: An Invitation to the Fair
lessons.summary: Maria visits her cousin at the county fair, watches his Welsh pony win a ribbon and sees a statue made of butter.
lessons.text:
In August, Maria received an invitation from her cousin Ben, who lived on a farm two hours from the city. The invitation was written by hand on a card with a drawing of a horse: "Come to the county fair! My pony is in the show on Saturday." Maria had never been to a county fair, and she accepted the invitation at once.

Ben's pony was a Welsh pony called Duke. Welsh ponies are small but strong, and the breed comes from the hills of Wales. Duke had a shiny brown coat, a long black tail and a proud way of holding his head. "He's the most handsome pony in the county," Ben said, and Maria had to agree. That morning Ben had washed and brushed him for two hours, so Duke looked even more handsome than usual.

The show took place in a large ring of sand. A judge in a white hat walked slowly around each pony. Ben explained the criteria to Maria: the judge looked at how the pony moved, how healthy it looked and how well it followed its young owner. "Looks are not one of the criteria," Ben said, "but they don't hurt." Duke followed every command, and Ben won a blue ribbon for the best Welsh pony of the day.

After the show, the cousins walked around the fair. The air smelled of sugar and hot oil, because almost everything was fried: fried chicken, fried potatoes, even fried candy bars. Ben said that people at the fair would fry anything. Maria ordered a plate of fries.

In one building, people stood in a long line to see a statue made entirely of butter. The statue showed a cow and her calf, life size, inside a cold glass room. Maria marveled at the details: you could even see the hair on the cow's ears. "Every year they make a new statue," Ben said, "and every year people marvel at it."

Next door, there was a pie contest. Visitors tasted small pieces of ten pies and then wrote the number of their favorite on a paper ballot. Maria chose an apple pie and filled in her ballot. Later, when all the ballots were counted, her favorite won.

When the sun went down, thousands of colored lights came on along the rides. The big wheel turned slowly against the dark sky. To Maria, the fair at night seemed almost magical. From the top of the wheel, she could see the whole fair shining below her, like a magical little city in the middle of the farms.

Questions:
Who sent Maria an invitation, and what was it for?
Her cousin Ben sent it, and it was an invitation to the county fair.
What kind of pony was Duke?
Duke was a Welsh pony with a shiny brown coat and a long black tail.
What criteria did the judge use?
The judge looked at how the pony moved, how healthy it looked and how well it followed its owner.
What was the statue made of?
It was made entirely of butter.
How did visitors choose the best pie?
They tasted the pies and wrote the number of their favorite on a paper ballot.

lessons.title: A Week at the Farm School
lessons.summary: A city boy spends a week at a farm school, sorts seeds, explores the woods and changes his mind about farm work.
lessons.text:
Jamal was 11 years old and had lived in Chicago all his life. In May, his class spent a week at a farm school in the country. The school was a real farm with cows, pigs and a large garden, where city children learned how food is grown.

On the first evening, the director, Ms Rivera, spoke briefly to the children. She did not give a long speech. She said only, "This week you will work, you will get dirty, and you will learn something." She had spoken so briefly that some children laughed, but Jamal liked her at once.

At first, Jamal thought the whole idea was nonsense. Why carry water to pigs when you can buy food at the store? "This is useless," he told his friend Leo on the second morning. "I'm never going to be a farmer." Leo agreed that it sounded like nonsense, but he went to work anyway.

The lessons were not what Jamal expected. On Tuesday, the children worked on a classification of seeds. Each group got a box of forty seeds and had to sort them into beans, grains and flower seeds. Many of the seeds looked almost the same, and they began to confuse Jamal. Ms Rivera showed the group a clever method: look at the shape first, then the color, then the size. "Small seeds confuse everyone at first," she said. With her clever method, the classification became much easier, and Jamal's group sorted every seed correctly.

On Wednesday, there was an exploration of the woods behind the farm. The children walked along a path, looking for animal tracks and birds' nests. During the exploration, Jamal found the tracks of a deer in the soft mud. Later, with the help of a book, he named them correctly.

Another thing that many city children find confusing is the difference between hay and straw. Ms Rivera explained it briefly: hay is dried grass that animals eat, while straw is the dry stems of grain that animals sleep on. Jamal repeated it until he could say it correctly.

On the last day, Jamal helped to pull carrots in the garden. That evening, they ate soup made from those carrots. As he ate, Jamal became conscious of something he had never thought about before: every meal begins with someone's work in a field. He was also conscious that he had changed his mind. The farm work was not useless at all.

Questions:
How did Ms Rivera speak to the children on the first evening?
She spoke briefly and did not give a long speech.
What did Jamal think of the farm school at first?
He thought the idea was nonsense and the work was useless.
What clever method did Ms Rivera show the group?
She told them to look at the shape first, then the color, then the size.
What did Jamal find during the exploration of the woods?
He found the tracks of a deer in the soft mud.
What is the difference between hay and straw?
Hay is dried grass that animals eat, and straw is the dry stems of grain that animals sleep on.
What did Jamal become conscious of on the last day?
He became conscious that every meal begins with someone's work in a field.

lessons.title: A Diary from the Country
lessons.summary: In her diary, a mother writes about her family's first months after moving from the city to a small farm.
lessons.text:
September 2

We moved into the old farm house today. For years, Dan and I had dreamed of leaving the city. Our apartment in Minneapolis was small, and the rent rose every year. Then Dan's company closed, and after six months of unemployment we knew that we could not stay. Homes in the city were no longer affordable for us, but out here a house with five acres of land is affordable, even on one salary. I am starting this diary because I want to remember everything about our first year.

September 10

Our daughter, Emma, who is thirteen, is finding it hard to cope. In the city she took the bus and the train everywhere on her own. Here there is no public transit at all, not even one bus a day. "Ugh, I have to ask you to drive me everywhere," she said this morning. "Ugh, I hate this." I told her that I am also learning to cope, one day at a time. In the city, transit was something we never thought about. Here, every trip needs a plan.

October 15

Dan started his new job at the high school today. His months of unemployment are finally over, and he came home smiling for the first time in a long while. He says the students call him "the city teacher."

November 8

Today something small happened that showed me the difference between the city and the country. I dropped my wallet in the parking lot of the grocery store in town, and I did not even notice. An hour later, the phone rang. A farmer had found my wallet, looked at my driver's license and called to say he would bring it to our house. In the city, I am sure I would never have seen that wallet again.

December 12

Last night the first snow fell. This morning a white blanket covered the fields, the fence and the roof of the barn. Emma ran outside in her boots and shouted, "It's beautiful!" It was the first time I had heard her say something good about the country. Dan drove her to school very slowly, so that they would arrive safely. Out here, everyone drives safely in winter, because the roads are covered with ice and the nearest hospital is forty minutes away.

Tonight, the three of us sat under a big wool blanket by the fire, and I wrote these lines in my diary. We are going to cope just fine.

Questions:
Why did the family leave the city?
Dan's company closed, and homes in the city were no longer affordable for them.
Why is Emma finding it hard to cope?
There is no public transit, so she has to ask her parents to drive her everywhere.
What happened to the mother's wallet?
She dropped it at the grocery store, and a farmer found it and brought it back.
What did the first snow look like?
It looked like a white blanket over the fields, the fence and the roof of the barn.
Why does everyone drive safely in winter?
The roads are covered with ice, and the nearest hospital is forty minutes away.

lessons.title: Bringing the Cattle Home
lessons.summary: After a football game, a young quarterback and his teammates help his family bring their cattle down from the mountains in Montana.
lessons.text:
On Friday night, Tyler Brooks played the most exciting football game of his life. He was the quarterback of his small high school team in Montana, and the game against their biggest rival went into overtime. In overtime, Tyler threw a long pass to his best friend, Cody, who caught it and scored. After the game, the young quarterback thanked his teammates. "I'll need you again tomorrow," he told them. "But not for football."

Tyler's family raised cattle at the foot of the mountains. Every summer, their three hundred cows lived high up in the hills, among tall pine trees and open grass. In October, before the first heavy snow, the family had to bring them down to the farm. An early storm in the mountains can be deadly for young calves, and in a bad year it can be deadly for older cows as well.

On Saturday morning, five of Tyler's teammates arrived, still tired from the game. Tyler's father gave each of them a horse. "Being a good teammate is useful up there," he joked, "but being a quarterback is not. Cows don't listen to quarterbacks."

Finding the cows was the hardest part. Some of them were hiding deep in the pine forest, where nobody could see them from the trail. So Tyler's sister, Megan, flew a small drone over the trees. On her screen, she could see brown shapes moving between the pines. With the help of the drone, the boys found every cow before lunch.

At lunch, Tyler's grandmother served beans, bread and hot coffee from her old chuck wagon. She explained to the boys that a chuck wagon was a kitchen on wheels, which cowboys used on long journeys with their cattle in the old days. Hers was more than a hundred years old.

In the afternoon, the cattle had to cross a highway. Two police officers came to escort them across the road. They stopped the traffic with their lights and escorted the long line of cows safely to the other side.

Back at the farm, the work was not finished. Each calf needed a vaccine against a common disease before winter. Tyler held the calves while his father gave each one its vaccine. Then a big truck arrived with a load of hay. Its engine had more than four hundred horsepower, which it needed to pull the heavy trailer up the wet road. Cody joked that the truck had more horsepower than their whole team.

That evening, the boys sat around a fire, tired and dirty. Cody said it had been harder than the game, even with the overtime.

Questions:
What happened in the football game on Friday night?
The game went into overtime, and Tyler threw a long pass to Cody, who scored.
Why did the family bring the cows down in October?
An early storm in the mountains can be deadly for young calves.
How did Megan help to find the cows in the pine forest?
She flew a small drone with a camera over the trees.
What is a chuck wagon?
It is a kitchen on wheels, which cowboys used on long journeys with their cattle.
What did each calf need before winter?
Each calf needed a vaccine against a common disease.

lessons.title: The Night of the Storm
lessons.summary: A family on a farm near the coast prepares for a hurricane, and the people nearby work together the next morning.
lessons.text:
Grace Miller lived with her parents and her little brother, Sam, on a small farm near the coast of North Carolina. From the top of their field, they could see the town harbor, where fishing boats rocked gently on the gray water.

One September morning, the news said that a hurricane was moving toward the coast. Grace and her father watched the weather radar on the television. On the radar, the hurricane looked like a huge white circle turning slowly over the ocean. "It will reach us tonight," her father said. "Not the center, but the edge." Every hour, Grace checked the radar again, and every hour the white circle was a little closer.

The family spent the whole day getting ready. Down in the harbor, the fishermen tied their boats with extra ropes and took the smallest ones out of the water. On the farm, the animals were the most vulnerable. The chickens lived in a low wooden house near the creek, which often flooded. Grace and her mother carried them, one by one, to the barn on higher ground. The young goats were vulnerable too, so they went into the barn with the chickens.

The storm arrived after dark. The wind roared around the house, and rain hit the windows like stones. At ten o'clock, the lights went out, and the television screen went blank. Grace's phone was blank too, because its battery was empty. Sam, who was seven, began to cry. Grace sat beside him with a flashlight and tried to console him. She told him stories about the goats and the chickens, safe and dry in the barn. Her mother consoled him too, and at last he fell asleep.

Toward morning, the wind gradually became weaker. When the sun came up, the storm was over. A few trees had fallen, and part of the barn roof was gone, but the animals were all safe. For several days, the river carried a huge discharge of brown water into the harbor. The discharge was so heavy that the fishing boats could not go out.

Gradually, life returned to normal. On the first dry morning, people from the farms nearby came over with tools and ladders to repair the barn roof. Later, the Millers helped the family next door clear the trees from their road. Grace had never seen such unity in her small town. Her father said that storms are terrible, but they remind people of their unity.

Questions:
What did the hurricane look like on the radar?
It looked like a huge white circle turning slowly over the ocean.
Why were the chickens vulnerable?
They lived in a low house near the creek, which often flooded.
What happened when the lights went out?
The television screen went blank, and Sam began to cry.
How did Grace console her brother?
She sat beside him with a flashlight and told him stories about the animals.
Why could the fishing boats not go out after the storm?
The river carried a huge discharge of brown water into the harbor.
What did the people from nearby farms do on the first dry morning?
They came with tools and ladders to repair the barn roof.

lessons.title: The Case of the Smelly Farm
lessons.summary: A short newspaper report on a lawsuit between new neighbors and an old dairy farm.
lessons.text:
A Farm, a Smell and a Lawsuit

A lawsuit that divided a quiet farming community ended last week, when both sides reached an agreement in the county court.

The case began two years ago. A couple from the city, Mark and Julie Fisher, bought a new house next to the Peterson family's dairy farm, which has been in the same family for four generations. Soon after they moved in, the Fishers complained about the strong smell from the farm and the noise of the machines early in the morning. When nothing changed, they filed a lawsuit against the farm.

The defendant in the case was Tom Peterson, who runs the farm with his two daughters. Because the farm and the house are both outside the city limits, the case came under the jurisdiction of the county court, not the city court. The judge said at the start that the county's jurisdiction was clear.

During the trial, the judge said that the Fishers' complaint was legitimate: living with a strong smell every day is a real problem, and legitimate problems deserve to be heard. However, the farm had followed every rule, and it had been there long before the new houses were built.

The court heard testimony from more than a dozen witnesses. Several people who live nearby gave testimony that the Petersons had always been helpful and honest. One woman said that Tom Peterson was "a man of complete integrity," and others spoke about his integrity in their testimony as well. An expert gave testimony about how modern farms can reduce smells.

The case also drew attention to a state law. Some years ago, the state legislature passed a "right to farm" law, which protects older farms from many complaints by people who move in later. Farmers' groups had lobbied hard for the law, and they are now lobbying the legislature to make it even stronger. Other groups say the law goes too far.

In the end, the defendant and the Fishers found a middle way. The Petersons agreed to plant a row of tall trees between the farm and the house and to start their machines an hour later. The Fishers agreed to drop the lawsuit. Before the agreement could take effect, the judge had to approve it. She praised both sides and said she was happy to approve an agreement that kept the peace.

The implications of the case go beyond one farm. As more city families move to the country, similar conflicts are likely. One implication, experts say, is that towns should plan more carefully where new houses are built.

Questions:
Why did the Fishers file a lawsuit?
They complained about the strong smell from the farm and the noise of the machines in the morning.
Who was the defendant in the case?
The defendant was Tom Peterson, who runs the farm with his two daughters.
Why was the case under the jurisdiction of the county court?
The farm and the house are both outside the city limits.
What did one woman say in her testimony?
She said that Tom Peterson was a man of complete integrity.
What did the two sides agree to do?
The Petersons agreed to plant trees and start their machines later, and the Fishers agreed to drop the lawsuit.

lessons.title: Sunshine on the Barn Roof
lessons.summary: A farmer explains in a column why she put solar panels on her farm and what they can and cannot do.
lessons.text:
Sunshine on the Barn Roof
By Linda Hayes

Last spring, my husband and I covered the roof of our barn with solar panels. Since then, people have stopped me at the grocery store, the post office and even at church to ask me about them. So I have decided to answer their questions here.

First, how does it work? On sunny days, the panels produce more power than our farm needs. The extra power goes into the electric grid, and the power company pays us for it. On cloudy days and at night, we take power back from the grid, just like before. The grid works a little like a bank: we put power in when we have extra, and we take it out when we need it.

Second, why did we do it? Partly for the money, of course. But we also wanted to cut our emissions. Farms produce more emissions than most people realize, from tractors, trucks and machines. We cannot remove all our emissions, but the panels have reduced them a great deal.

Third, was it difficult? The paperwork was the hardest part. Our first submission to the county was returned because one drawing was missing. Our second submission was complete, and the county board sanctioned the project two months later. Once the plan was sanctioned, the work took only three weeks.

What surprised us most was the integration of the panels into our daily work. We worried that they would get in the way. Instead, the integration was easy. The panels on the barn roof do not take any land, and we have also put a few panels in a field where our sheep eat the grass underneath them.

Of course, solar power has its limitations. The most obvious limitation is that the panels produce nothing at night and very little under heavy snow. In our part of the country, that is a real limitation from December to February.

Finally, I like to think of our farm as a portfolio. A smart investor never puts all her money in one place, and a smart farmer should not depend on one source of income. Our portfolio now includes milk, hay, a few sheep and sunshine. In a bad year for milk prices, the sun still shines.

Questions:
What happens to the extra power from the panels?
It goes into the electric grid, and the power company pays for it.
Why did Linda and her husband want solar panels?
They wanted to save money and to cut the farm's emissions.
Why was their first submission returned?
It was returned because one drawing was missing.
What is the biggest limitation of solar power?
The panels produce nothing at night and very little under heavy snow.
Why does Linda think of her farm as a portfolio?
A smart farmer should not depend on one source of income, just as a smart investor does not put all her money in one place.

lessons.title: Summer on a Revolutionary Farm
lessons.summary: An exchange student spends a summer as a guide on a historic farm and learns the story of the family who lived there.
lessons.text:
My name is Lucia, and I am a history student from Spain. Last summer, I came to the United States on a student visa to work as a guide at a historic farm in New England. Getting the visa took three months of forms and one long interview, but as soon as I saw the farm, I knew it had been worth it.

The farm is a living museum. It looks exactly as it did around 1776, during the Revolutionary War. The guides wear clothes from that time, cook over an open fire and work the fields with horses. During the Revolutionary War, the family who lived here grew food for the soldiers, and their oldest son, Samuel, joined the revolutionary army when he was only seventeen.

The house itself is humble. It has two rooms downstairs, two small bedrooms under the roof and a kitchen with a huge stone fireplace. There is no electricity, so every evening I lit the oil lamps. The soft light of the lamps made the humble rooms feel warm and safe. Visitors often told me that they could imagine the family sitting there, two hundred and fifty years ago.

My favorite part of the job was telling visitors about the war. At that time, the colonies were still part of an empire ruled from London. The imperial government there made the laws and decided the taxes, and many farmers felt that the imperial rulers did not care about their lives. That anger grew, year by year, until it led to war.

The museum has custody of more than one hundred letters that the family wrote during the war. They are kept in a cool, dark room, and only the director can take them out. One afternoon, she let me read a few of them. The museum's custody of the letters is a serious responsibility, she explained, because they are the only copies in the world.

In one letter, Samuel wrote to his mother from the army camp. He said that he missed the farm and her cooking, but that he believed it was his destiny to fight for a free country. Reading his words, I felt that the young farmer was speaking directly to me. I do not know if I believe in destiny, but when my visa ended and I flew home, I took a small part of that humble farm with me.

Questions:
Why did Lucia come to the United States?
She came on a student visa to work as a guide at a historic farm.
What did Samuel do during the Revolutionary War?
He joined the revolutionary army when he was only seventeen.
What did Lucia do every evening in the house?
She lit the oil lamps, because there was no electricity.
Why did many farmers feel angry with the imperial government?
They felt that the imperial rulers in London did not care about their lives.
Why is the museum's custody of the letters a serious responsibility?
The letters are the only copies in the world.
What did Samuel believe was his destiny?
He believed it was his destiny to fight for a free country.
